105.history: The straight town on the west coast took in the first human families to settle beside the Dia-thìrich rather than apart from them. Samuel Hale tightened herring barrels on its quay, Torcall the mason witnessed in its Dia-thìreach book, and a marriage was made there in two tongues. The town was governed for a long season by a joint council of both peoples, six of each, and lost its harbour dues to the Company in the years of the Levy. Thomas Hale first set his name to paper against the Administration here. In the last autumn each side asked the children of the old council which people they were, and most would not answer; Eilidh Hale kept the books and stayed. Its quay is a single long street down to the water, and the humans' slip where the first boat was launched stood at its foot. The storm of the wolf-moon drowned men of both peoples off its harbour in one night, and both were lit for at the lamps of the drowned.
105.known_for: the joint council and its children

134.history: The harbour town up the western coast heard of the three ships within two days of their coming, and its custodian rode south to see them. In the first years of the strangers Torcall the mason set a new stone face on its harbour wall, and when a human supply-brig broke on the reefs south of the town its custodian gave the drowned ground above the tide-line among the dunes. The town kept that ground apart for the strangers' dead for the rest of the age. The custodian who rode south in the first year to see the ships wrote the only account of them from the western coast, and it was her successor who asked Torcall to mend the wall.
134.known_for: the strangers' graves in the dunes

1.history: The town on the wide strait took its tolls from the strangers' shipping as it had from the western pilots, and for two generations its merchants sold wool by the Company's weight and at the Company's price. When the humans' ships thinned in the years before the war, the wool piled in its warehouses and the merchants quietly began to sell inland again, against the letter of the law. By the war its harbour stood idle. The tally-book of Pike's post named its merchants the hardest bargainers on the island, since they would take only iron by weight for their wool, and they sent the first wool-ship to the humans' post in the treaty's second year.

398.history: The large village of the red well gave its name to Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, the last of the five lights as the ring is counted round the coast from Baile chrom. Its first keeper was chosen by the Administration on the custodians' word. In the first spring of the war its keeper Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill put the light out with her own hand, before any order reached her, rather than guide the Company's ships along a coast the council held; when the truce was signed the council had it lit again. The keeper's daybook there ends its entries for the war with a line of Raonaid's own, and takes them up again without comment at the relighting.
398.known_for: the light put out in the war

26.history: The deep city on the lake shore, five miles from the capital by the lake road, holds the first building the strangers ever owned outright on Dia-thìr: the stone warehouse Pike raised there in the treaty's first summer to keep A' Chompanaidh's tools out of reach of the harbour thieves of Ros dhomhain. The Company's surgeon came to its sick only once in the strangers' fever, and it was here that Anne Colby first wrote the dead by name. In the rising the townsfolk broke the warehouse open and carried off its rope, nails and powder for the council's companies, and left its doors swinging. The fishing town runs down to the shore beside the capital's deep water, and the old folk there said the warehouse door was the first door on the island ever hung with a lock the town could not open.

433.history: The walled town of the Stone, where the panther road passes, did in the first fever years what the hills only talked of: it turned the fever back at its gates. The Administration fined it for hindering trade, and it paid the fine in wool, more sacks than the humans knew what to do with. Its priests kept the oldest shrines of Òrd na Cloiche open through all the age. Its wool fine was long told in the south-west as the one bargain the humans ever lost by weight.
